question: The state postulate says a simple compressible substance's equilibrium states form a single two-dimensional surface in (P, v, T) space. Given the values of any two independent intensive variables -- say P and T -- what does the state postulate say about the rest?

answers.answer: v (and every other equilibrium property) is already fixed -- the two you chose pick out one point on the surface, and a point on a surface has no remaining freedom.
answers.feedback: Right. That is exactly what "a single two-dimensional surface" means: two coordinates locate a point on it, and the third coordinate is then read off, not separately chosen.

answers.answer: P, v and T are three fully independent knobs, so all three must be measured separately.
answers.feedback: This is what the state postulate denies. If P, v and T were independent, equilibrium states would fill a three-dimensional volume, not sit on a two-dimensional surface -- and there would be no such thing as "the equation of state".

answers.answer: Only extensive variables like V and N determine the state; P and T alone are not enough.
answers.feedback: Backwards. P and T (both intensive) are exactly what the state postulate says suffices to fix v; N sets how much substance you have, not which point on the per-particle surface it occupies.

answers.answer: This is true only for the ideal gas; real gases need a third independent variable.
answers.feedback: The state postulate is a general claim about any simple compressible substance's equilibrium surface -- the van der Waals gas included. It does not add a degree of freedom the ideal gas lacked.

question: You have a gas bottle at (N, V, T). You open a valve to an identical second bottle at the same state, merging into one system with twice the gas, in twice the volume, at the same T. Which of the following correctly lists what changes?

answers.answer: V, N and U (the internal energy) double; P and T stay exactly the same.
answers.feedback: Correct -- the doubling test: extensive quantities (V, N, U) double, intensive quantities (P, T, and v = V/N) do not move at all.

answers.answer: P, V, T and N all double.
answers.feedback: Doubling P and T along with V and N would make "the pressure of the gas" depend on how much gas happened to be in the room -- which cannot be right, since two adjacent litres of the same gas at the same temperature must report the same pressure.

answers.answer: Nothing changes -- joining two identical systems just makes a bigger version of the same state.
answers.feedback: V, N and U genuinely double; the two halves really do add up to twice the substance. Only the intensive quantities (P, T, v) stay fixed, not everything.

answers.answer: Only T changes, since heat flows between the two halves until they equilibrate.
answers.feedback: The two halves start at the same T, so there is nothing to equilibrate -- T was never going to move, and neither was P.

question: A room measures 30 m^3 and holds air at 101325 Pa and 293 K. Using P V = N k_B T with k_B = 1.381e-23 J/K, how many gas particles does the room contain?

answers.feedback: N = P V / (k_B T) = (101325)(30) / [(1.381e-23)(293)] = 7.51e26 particles -- the same calculation as P V = N k_B T, solved for N instead of P.

question: CO2 gas at 280 K is compressed slowly at fixed temperature, well past several times its critical volume. Which best describes what a pressure gauge on the container actually reads, compared with the ideal-gas prediction P = k_B T / v?

answers.answer: The measured pressure climbs more slowly than the ideal prediction, then plateaus at the substance's saturation pressure while the ideal prediction keeps climbing without limit.
answers.feedback: Right -- this is exactly what the NIST CO2 isotherm data in this module shows: the real gas departs from P = k_B T / v well before condensation, and then flattens into a plateau the ideal law has no mechanism to produce at all.

answers.answer: The measured pressure tracks P = k_B T / v exactly at any density, since every gas obeys the ideal gas law.
answers.feedback: This is exactly the claim the module's NIST CO2 data falsifies. The ideal gas law contains no substance-specific constant, so it cannot know that CO2 condenses -- real CO2's measured pressure departs sharply from the ideal prediction long before the plateau, let alone during it.

answers.answer: The measured pressure rises faster than the ideal prediction at every volume.
answers.feedback: Attraction dominates over most of the compression, which *lowers* the measured pressure below the ideal prediction, not raises it -- only deep in the compressed liquid does pressure rise steeply.

answers.answer: The measured pressure drops to zero once the substance starts to condense.
answers.feedback: Condensation holds the pressure at a constant, nonzero value -- the saturation pressure -- not zero. A pressure of zero would mean no gas left at all.

question: Using a, b fit from CO2's measured critical point (T_c = 304.13 K, P_c = 7.3773e6 Pa, via a = 27(k_B T_c)^2/(64 P_c), b = k_B T_c/(8 P_c)), compute the van der Waals pressure at a molar volume of 1.2e-3 m^3/mol (per-particle v = V_m/N_A) and T = 280 K. Give the signed fractional deviation from the ideal prediction k_B T/v at the same state (negative if the van der Waals pressure is lower).

answers.feedback: Ideal: P = k_B T/v ~= 1.940e6 Pa. Van der Waals: P ~= 1.758e6 Pa. The attraction term a/v^2 dominates at this density -- the excluded-volume correction 1/(v-b) is still close to 1/v since v is far larger than b here -- so the net shift is negative, about -9.4%, well before condensation is anywhere in sight.

question: A gas has per-particle van der Waals constants a = 1.0037e-48 Pa m^6 and b = 7.0855e-29 m^3 (converted from independently published textbook molar constants for CO2, not fit from its critical point). Using k_B T_c = 8a/(27b), compute T_c in kelvin.

answers.feedback: T_c = 8a/(27 k_B b) ~= 304.0 K -- within 0.1% of CO2's measured critical temperature, 304.13 K, even though a and b here came from an independent fit, not from the critical point itself. P_c = a/(27 b^2) ~= 7.40e6 Pa lands within about half a percent of the measured 7.3773e6 Pa the same way.

question: Two different gases -- say CO2 and N2 -- are held at the same reduced temperature T_r and the same reduced pressure P_r, even though their critical points (and their a, b) are completely different numbers. Do the two gases have the same compressibility factor Z, or does Z depend on which gas it is?

answers.answer: The same Z -- the law of corresponding states says any van der Waals substance at a given (T_r, P_r) has the same reduced volume v_r, and Z is built entirely out of reduced quantities once P_c v_c/(k_B T_c) = 3/8 is used to eliminate the substance- specific constants.
answers.feedback: Correct. P_r = 8T_r/(3v_r - 1) - 3/v_r^2 has no a, b or N_A left in it at all, so fixing (T_r, P_r) fixes v_r -- and hence Z -- the same way for every van der Waals substance, regardless of its own critical point.

answers.answer: Z depends on the gas's chemistry, so it is never the same for two different gases.
answers.feedback: This is true of the *un-reduced* pressure -- two gases at the same (v, T) generally have different P, because a and b differ. But once P, v and T are measured in units of each gas's own critical point, that substance-specific information cancels out of the reduced equation entirely.

answers.answer: The same Z, but only because CO2 and N2 happen to have similar molecular masses -- for a very different pair of gases it would not hold.
answers.feedback: The law of corresponding states does not depend on molecular mass, or on any property of the two gases matching -- it follows from a, b cancelling out of the reduced van der Waals equation algebraically, for any pair of substances at all.

answers.answer: Only if both gases are measured at exactly their own critical points, T_r = P_r = 1.
answers.feedback: The reduced equation holds at every (T_r, P_r), not only at the critical point -- T_r = P_r = 1 is just the one point every reduced isotherm is required to pass through, by construction.
